source.title: Augment Your Batch: Improving Generalization Through Instance Repetition
source.authors: Elad Hoffer; Tal Ben-Nun; Itay Hubara; Niv Giladi; T. Hoefler; Daniel Soudry

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper, though its displayed title differs from the catalog title. It includes flattened tables and figure descriptions.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether a large-batch training penalty can be reduced using batch augmentation, and reports results that qualify the claim: batch augmentation improves validation performance under its tested settings, while the comparison to regime adaptation shows mixed outcomes across models.
record.gate_note: The paper's own batch-augmentation and regime-adaptation comparisons bear on V5. Statements about other large-batch studies in the introduction and references are cited prior work, not rows. Gradient-correlation and gradient-norm measurements support the paper's analysis but do not measure the training-to-test gap named in the claim versions, so they are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures held-out performance as effective batch size increases through repeated augmented instances, usually holding epochs and learning rates fixed. It tests V5's recipe-adaptation qualification, rather than directly replicating a conventional batch-size sweep.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that repeating differently augmented instances within each batch improves final held-out performance and convergence per epoch across their tested models. They argue that this permits larger effective batches and, with schedule adaptation, fewer updates to a target accuracy. They do not establish that conventional large batches of distinct examples improve generalization without adaptation.
record.recipe_differences: The study tests batch augmentation, which repeats each sample in a batch with different transformations, rather than the original fixed-epoch batch-size comparison; some evaluations hold the number of epochs fixed, while others adapt the training schedule.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with model, dataset, augmentation, multiplier M, training schedule, and whether the comparison is against regime adaptation. The paper reports stronger gains for some settings than others.
record.problems: Most reported outcomes are validation accuracy or test perplexity, not train-to-test error gaps; several curve comparisons are available only as figures without numerical values. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the accuracy table. The reported comparisons use selected models and settings rather than a systematic batch-size sweep.
record.rows_left_out: No required result rows omitted. Gradient-correlation measurements in Table 1 and gradient-norm comparisons in Figures 2 and 6 were not included because they do not measure the training-to-test gap or another behavior named by the claim versions. Throughput-only results in Table 2 were also excluded.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting versus natural-label held-out accuracy.
Width increases beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and learned local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and effects of tuning.

The onset of the conventional large-batch penalty under a systematic fixed-epoch sweep of distinct-example batch sizes; learning-rate scaling and warmup as remedies. BA keeps distinct examples per update and updates per epoch fixed while increasing augmented instances.
Adding versus removing dropout, small-data effects, excessive dropout, and joint removal with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness rankings of generalization gaps and comparisons with other measures.
Removing memorized training examples versus random examples.

missing.what: Omitted CIFAR-10 baseline-to-BA accuracy comparisons: ResNet44 93.07%→93.78% (M=40); VGG+cutout 93.82%→95.32% (M=32); Wide-ResNet28-10+cutout 96.6%→97.15% (M=6); DARTS 97.11%→97.64% (M=10).

All CIFAR-100 baseline-to-BA comparisons are missing: ResNet44+cutout 72.97%→74.13% (M=40); VGG+cutout 73.03%→75.5% (M=32); Wide-ResNet28-10+cutout 79.85%→80.13% (M=10); DenseNet100-12 77.73%→78.8% (M=4). These extend the tested setting beyond those recorded.
ImageNet MobileNet accuracy improves from 70.6% to 71.4% with M=4 under the original training regime.

Shortened-schedule results: CIFAR-10 ResNet44+cutout reaches 94.15% in 23 epochs with BA, larger learning rate and faster decay versus the stated 93.07% baseline in 100 epochs; the baseline degrades under the shortened regime. ImageNet ResNet50 with BA reaches 76.86% in 40 epochs or 75.7% in 23 epochs after schedule adaptation. These quantify adaptation's training-budget consequences.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text identifies itself as arXiv:1901.09335v1, dated January 2019; its binding to the supplied CVPR DOI cannot be verified here. It is not among the listed original sources. Small gains over baseline do not warrant partial states when the tested V5 outcome is avoiding a large-batch penalty. Accuracy tables provide no uncertainty estimates.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Generalization as network width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classification.
The paper tests batch augmentation and regime adaptation on selected image and language tasks; it does not report a systematic fixed-epoch batch-size sweep across image and language models.
Dropout's direct effect on test error and its interaction with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.
